edits.why_wrong: A. Rotavirus causes gastroenteritis in young children. C. Respiratory syncytial virus causes bronchiolitis and respiratory infections, not temporal lobe encephalitis. D. Hepatitis A causes acute hepatitis. E. Norovirus causes vomiting and diarrhoea.
edits.why_correct: Herpes simplex virus is the commonest identified cause of sporadic viral encephalitis in the UK. It has a predilection for the temporal lobes, producing personality change, confusion and seizures. Intravenous aciclovir should be started immediately and CSF sent for HSV PCR. Source: NHS, Encephalitis, 2023.

issues: Clinically correct (CRS triad after first-trimester rubella; MMR is live, avoid pregnancy for one month after). Distractors weak but not wrong. Borderline overlap with live BX773 (why rubella exposure in pregnancy matters), which does not test the CRS features, so kept. Added Source line and sources.

edits.why_correct: Rubella in the first trimester can cross the placenta and cause congenital rubella syndrome. The classic features are sensorineural deafness, congenital heart disease such as patent ductus arteriosus, and eye defects including cataracts. The risk of defects is highest when infection occurs early in pregnancy. Source: UKHSA, Green Book chapter 28: Rubella, updated 2026.

Correct and current; no live repeat found. Added Source line and sources.

edits.why_correct: Barrier methods such as male and female condoms are the only contraceptives that also reduce the transmission of sexually transmitted infections. She can use condoms alone or alongside a more reliable hormonal or intrauterine method for extra pregnancy protection. Free condoms are available from sexual health services. Source: NICE CKS, Contraception - barrier methods and spermicides, 2026.

issues: Key correct (NICE NG33: HIV-positive people with latent TB are at increased risk of active disease). Key was the longest option; shortened. why_wrong D made more precise: ART is started during TB treatment, earliest when CD4 is very low; "usually within the first weeks" was imprecise for higher CD4 counts. Added Source line and sources.

options.A: Tuberculosis in people with HIV is usually confined to the lungs
options.B: Sputum smears are more likely to be positive as immunosuppression advances
options.C: HIV-related immunosuppression greatly increases progression from latent to active tuberculosis
options.D: Antiretroviral therapy should be withheld until the full course of tuberculosis treatment is finished
options.E: Contact tracing is unnecessary because co-infected patients cannot transmit tuberculosis

edits.correct_answer: C. HIV-related immunosuppression greatly increases progression from latent to active tuberculosis
edits.why_wrong: A. Extrapulmonary and disseminated tuberculosis become more common, not less, as the CD4 count falls. B. Advanced HIV produces fewer cavities, so smear-negative disease is more frequent. D. Antiretroviral therapy is started during tuberculosis treatment rather than after it, earliest of all when the CD4 count is very low, because this improves survival. E. Pulmonary disease in co-infected patients can still be infectious, so contacts must be assessed.
edits.why_correct: Loss of CD4 cell-mediated immunity removes the main defence that keeps Mycobacterium tuberculosis contained in granulomas, so people with HIV are many times more likely to develop active disease, either from reactivation of latent infection or rapid progression of new infection. Disease is also more often extrapulmonary or disseminated. This is why everyone with tuberculosis should be offered an HIV test, and why co-infected patients need joint specialist care. Source: NICE NG33 Tuberculosis, 2016 (updated 2024).

issues: Duplicate: near-identical scenario and learning point to u74-g13 PAN8305 (admitted man, months of cough/sweats, upper-lobe cavitation on CXR -> single side room with airborne precautions rather than an open bay); also repeats PAN1303 in this batch. Cross-batch coordination needed: keep only one.

Correct. Same diagnosis as parked PAQ240 but a different scenario (simultaneous household cluster rather than a single returning traveller), so kept; PAN6366 in this batch dropped as the repeat. Added Source line and sources.

edits.why_correct: Abrupt vomiting and watery stools affecting a whole family within a day or two points to a transmissible infection, most often viral, spread person to person or through shared food. Chronic bowel conditions develop over weeks to months in one individual and would not appear simultaneously in four people. Source: NICE CKS, Gastroenteritis, 2026.

issues: Correct; no live repeat found. Reworded "notifiable to UKHSA" (notification goes to the local health protection team). Added Source line and sources.

edits.why_correct: Fever, abdominal cramps and diarrhoea starting a day or so after eating raw or undercooked egg is a classic picture of non-typhoidal Salmonella gastroenteritis. A second case linked to the same food supports a foodborne source. Most cases settle with fluids alone, and food poisoning is notifiable, so the local health protection team should be informed. Source: NHS, Food poisoning, 2024; UKHSA, Notifiable diseases and causative organisms, 2025.

issues: Duplicate: fever, cramps and diarrhoea turning bloody a few days after undercooked barbecue chicken -> Campylobacter. Same scenario and learning point as parked PAQ15651 and u74-g11 PAN3790 (pink barbecue chicken -> Campylobacter jejuni).

Correct (loss of colonisation resistance; NICE NG199/CKS risk factors incl. clindamycin, cephalosporins, co-amoxiclav, quinolones and PPIs). Key was the longest option; shortened key and lengthened A. No live item tests the mechanism (BX137 tests the risk factor). Added Source line and sources.

options.A: Antibiotics directly ulcerate the colonic lining, which then becomes secondarily infected
options.B: Antibiotics kill protective gut bacteria, letting C. difficile multiply and make toxins
options.C: Antibiotics trigger an allergic reaction in the colon that mimics infection
options.D: Antibiotics carry C. difficile spores into the bowel from the tablet coating
options.E: Antibiotics make C. difficile invade the bloodstream and seed the colon

edits.correct_answer: B. Antibiotics kill protective gut bacteria, letting C. difficile multiply and make toxins
edits.why_correct: The healthy colonic microbiota resists colonisation by C. difficile. Antibiotics, especially broad-spectrum agents, disrupt this flora, so ingested spores can germinate, multiply and release toxins A and B that damage the colon. Avoiding antibiotics that are not needed is therefore a key part of preventing first and recurrent episodes. Source: NICE NG199 Clostridioides difficile infection: antimicrobial prescribing, 2021; NICE CKS, Diarrhoea - antibiotic associated, 2025.

issues: Duplicate: inpatient with new diarrhoea and suspected C. difficile -> single room, contact precautions, soap-and-water hand washing, sporicidal cleaning. Same scenario and learning point as parked PAQ15368 and PAN1570, and u74-g13 PAN1572 and PAN1022 (both in g13 check list).

Correct; no repeat found. Softened illness duration to match UK factsheets (usually about 1-2 weeks). The stem line about chlorine resistance strongly cues the answer but is acceptable. Added Source line and sources.

edits.why_correct: Cryptosporidium is a protozoan whose oocysts resist chlorine, so it is the classic cause of outbreaks linked to swimming pools and water supplies. It causes watery diarrhoea and cramps that usually settle within a couple of weeks in immunocompetent people. Diagnosis is by stool testing (antigen, PCR or microscopy) for Cryptosporidium, and linked cases are investigated by the local health protection team. Source: Public Health Agency Northern Ireland, Cryptosporidium factsheet, 2025.

issues: Duplicate: profuse watery diarrhoea with dry mouth, light-headedness and low urine output -> dehydration. Same learning point and similar scenario to parked PAN8433 and PAN8203 (after holiday abroad -> dehydration with electrolyte disturbance); u74-g07 PAN8907 also covers it.
Correct. Live BX826 tests faecal-oral spread of hepatitis A specifically, a different fact, so kept. Added Source line and sources.

edits.why_correct: Outbreaks of vomiting and diarrhoea are usually caused by organisms passed from faeces to the mouth through contaminated hands, food or water. Missing soap and a shared tap for drinking and washing up provide exactly these routes. Hand hygiene with soap and water and safe food and water handling are the key control measures. Source: NICE CKS, Gastroenteritis, 2026.

issues: Correct; no repeat of miliary TB found. Added Source line and sources.

edits.why_correct: Miliary tuberculosis results from haematogenous spread of Mycobacterium tuberculosis, seeding many organs at once. The diffuse 'millet seed' nodules on chest X-ray, abnormal liver tests and choroidal tubercles in an immunosuppressed man from a high-incidence country fit dissemination rather than localised lung disease. It is a medical emergency needing prompt specialist treatment. Source: NICE NG33 Tuberculosis, 2016 (updated 2024).

Correct (NICE NG95 lists facial palsy as a focal presentation of Lyme disease). Live DS111 covers treatment of Lyme facial palsy with the diagnosis given, and erythema migrans items cover the rash, so this diagnosis item is kept. Added Source line and sources.

edits.why_correct: Lyme disease, caused by Borrelia burgdorferi from tick bites, can cause neurological involvement weeks after the initial rash, and facial nerve palsy is the commonest cranial neuropathy. An outdoor worker in a tick area with a previous expanding ring-shaped rash, arthralgia and lower motor neurone facial weakness fits early disseminated Lyme disease. Source: NICE NG95 Lyme disease, 2018.

edits.why_correct: Skin commensals such as coagulase-negative staphylococci can easily enter the bottles if technique is poor, giving false-positive cultures. Contaminated results lead to unnecessary antibiotics, extra tests, longer stays and confusion about the true cause of sepsis, so aseptic non-touch technique protects the accuracy of the result. Source: UK Standards for Microbiology Investigations B 37, Investigation of blood cultures, UKHSA, 2024.

issues: Duplicate: suspected bacterial meningitis -> IV ceftriaxone immediately, not delayed for CT/LP. Same scenario and learning point as live NEU036 and ID014; u74-g13 PAN965 also covers the LP-versus-antibiotics angle.

Reinstated: partner g11 PAN3781 dropped. Full check: clinically correct. UKHSA says the incubation is usually 3 to 12 weeks (here seven weeks), early anxiety and fever are followed by swallowing spasm (hydrophobia), and rabies is almost invariably fatal once symptoms appear; aerophobia is a classic sign. Repeat check against live, held and kept items only: live BX186 (wound first aid) and parked PAQ15267 (urgent post-exposure risk assessment) test exposure management, not recognition of clinical rabies; live ID046 is cat-bite antibiotics; g11 PAN3781, PAN7708 and PAN10107 were all dropped. Not a repeat. Option lengths already pass (key "Rabies" is the shortest option), so the options are unchanged. Added Source line and sources.

edits.why_correct: Rabies is a lyssavirus infection transmitted by bites from infected mammals, particularly dogs in endemic regions. After an incubation of weeks to months it causes encephalitis with agitation, hydrophobia and aerophobia from pharyngeal spasm. Once symptoms appear it is almost always fatal, so post-exposure prophylaxis after any potential exposure is vital. Source: UKHSA, Rabies: epidemiology, transmission and prevention, 2025; UKHSA, Rabies risk assessment, post-exposure treatment and management, 2026.

Key was the longest option by far (50 vs 20) and read as a category. Rewrote options: key now "Chikungunya virus infection"; septic arthritis replaced by disseminated gonococcal infection (excluded by no new sexual partners or discharge), others reworded. why_correct, why_wrong, thinking and exam_trap updated to match. Checked against UKHSA chikungunya guidance.

edits.why_correct: Fever, rash and acute symmetrical polyarthritis of the small joints after many mosquito bites in the Caribbean is typical of chikungunya, an alphavirus spread by Aedes mosquitoes. Joint pain can be severe and may persist for weeks to months. Dengue and Zika can look similar, and malaria should still be excluded when travel has been to an endemic area. Source: UKHSA, Chikungunya guidance, 2025.
edits.why_wrong: A. Disseminated gonococcal infection causes tenosynovitis, a sparse pustular rash and arthritis after a recent sexual exposure, which he denies. C. Reactive arthritis follows gut or genital infection and is usually an asymmetrical large-joint oligoarthritis. D. Gout rarely starts in several small joints at once and does not cause a widespread rash with fever. E. Rheumatoid arthritis develops more gradually and is not accompanied by an acute febrile rash.
edits.thinking: Recent Caribbean travel with mosquito bites  ↓  Fever and widespread rash  ↓  Acute symmetrical small-joint polyarthritis  ↓  No gut, genital or sexual trigger  ↓  Chikungunya
edits.exam_trap: C, Post-infective reactive arthritis — joint symptoms after travel suggest it, but there was no preceding diarrhoea or genital infection and the pattern is symmetrical small-joint disease with a rash.

edits.why_correct: A flu-like or glandular-fever-like illness with rash, mouth ulcers and generalised lymphadenopathy two to four weeks after a sexual exposure is the typical picture of HIV seroconversion. A negative glandular fever screen makes EBV less likely. She should be offered a fourth-generation HIV test (antigen and antibody), which detects infection early; viral load is very high at this stage, so early diagnosis also reduces onward transmission. Source: NICE CKS, HIV infection and AIDS, 2025; BHIVA, UK guidelines for HIV testing, 2020.

edits.why_correct: Streptococcus pneumoniae is the commonest cause of bacterial meningitis in adults in the UK. Spread from a contiguous focus such as otitis media is a classic route, and pneumococci appear as Gram-positive diplococci on CSF microscopy. Pneumococcal meningitis carries a high mortality and risk of hearing loss, which is why dexamethasone is given alongside antibiotics. Source: NICE NG240 Meningitis (bacterial) and meningococcal disease, 2024.

edits.stem:
At an urgent treatment centre, a 30-year-old woman who missed her childhood immunisations is seen with four days of fever, a runny nose, a hacking cough and sore red eyes. Today a blotchy red rash appeared at her hairline and is spreading down her body. Small white spots are seen on the inside of her cheeks.

What is the most appropriate immediate action?

options.A: Return her to the shared waiting area wearing a surgical face mask
options.B: Keep her in the waiting room until her measles test result returns
options.C: Move her promptly to a single room away from other patients
options.D: Start oral phenoxymethylpenicillin for presumed scarlet fever
options.E: Give a dose of MMR vaccine now to shorten the illness

edits.correct_answer: C. Move her promptly to a single room away from other patients
edits.why_correct: A prodrome of fever, cough, coryza and conjunctivitis followed by a rash spreading down from the hairline, with Koplik spots, makes measles very likely in this unimmunised adult. Measles spreads by the airborne route and is extremely infectious, so the immediate priority is to move her out of shared areas into a single room with the door closed. Staff should then notify the local health protection team on clinical suspicion and arrange testing, without waiting for confirmation. Source: UKHSA, National measles guidelines version 8, 2026.
edits.why_wrong: A. A surgical mask does not make it safe for someone with an airborne infection such as measles to share a waiting area with vulnerable patients. B. Waiting for a result before isolating her exposes others, including pregnant women and infants, while she is highly infectious. D. Cough, conjunctivitis and Koplik spots point to measles rather than scarlet fever, so antibiotics are not indicated. E. MMR given to someone already ill with measles does not change the course; post-exposure MMR is for susceptible contacts.
edits.thinking: Unimmunised adult  ↓  Fever with cough, coryza and conjunctivitis  ↓  Rash spreading down from the hairline with Koplik spots  ↓  Measles is airborne and highly infectious  ↓  Isolate in a single room now, then notify
edits.exam_trap: A, A mask in the waiting area — masks help with droplet infections, but measles is airborne and she needs a single room away from others.

issues: Duplicate: teenager with hours of fever, leg pains, headache and non-blanching purpura -> meningococcal disease. Same scenario and learning point as live PAN3342 (16-year-old with leg pains and non-blanching spots), live BX420/BX946, parked PAQ15748 and PAN6641.

Correct. Key was the longest option; shortened to "Exactly where and when he travelled" (why_correct still explains destinations and dates). Distractors are implausible but not wrong. Added Source line and sources.

options.A: The airline and class of seat he flew in
options.B: Whether he has valid travel insurance
options.C: Exactly where and when he travelled
options.D: The brand of sun cream he used
options.E: Whether he ate any spicy food abroad

edits.correct_answer: C. Exactly where and when he travelled
edits.why_correct: Malaria risk depends on where someone has been, including rural or urban areas within a country, and when. Knowing exact destinations confirms whether he entered an endemic area, and the dates show whether the timing fits the incubation period; falciparum usually presents within weeks, while vivax and ovale can relapse months later. This history guides the urgency of blood films and specialist advice. Source: UKHSA, Malaria prevention guidelines for travellers from the UK, 2026.

issues: Correct (avoid aspirin and other NSAIDs, use paracetamol). Borderline overlap with live ID026 (dengue diagnosis plus "supportive care, no NSAIDs"); kept because this item tests the drug-safety point on its own in a telephone-advice scenario, but flagged for the human reviewer to decide. Added Source line and sources.

edits.why_correct: Dengue can cause thrombocytopenia and, in severe forms, plasma leakage and bleeding. Aspirin and other NSAIDs impair platelet function and increase the risk of haemorrhage, so they should be avoided until dengue has been excluded. Paracetamol at standard doses and good oral hydration are the mainstays of symptom relief, with medical review for warning signs such as abdominal pain, persistent vomiting or bleeding. Source: nidirect (NHS information, Northern Ireland), Dengue, accessed 2026; UKHSA, Dengue fever guidance, 2025.

issues: Correct; no repeat found. why_wrong D reworded ("E. coli" read as an explanation of key letter E). Added Source line and sources.

edits.why_wrong: A. Campylobacter has an incubation of several days and causes fever and often bloody diarrhoea. B. Salmonella usually starts 12 to 72 hours after eating, with fever and diarrhoea. C. Clostridium perfringens typically causes diarrhoea and cramps 8 to 16 hours after reheated meat dishes, with little vomiting. D. Escherichia coli O157 has an incubation of several days and causes bloody diarrhoea with a risk of haemolytic uraemic syndrome.
edits.why_correct: Staphylococcus aureus from an infected skin lesion on a food handler can contaminate food, multiply at room temperature and produce a heat-stable preformed enterotoxin. Because the toxin is already present, vomiting begins within a few hours of eating and settles within about a day without fever. Cold meats, sandwiches and cream products are typical vehicles. Source: UKHSA, Notifiable diseases and causative organisms, 2025; NHS, Food poisoning, 2024.

issues: Correct; no repeat found. Added Source line and sources.

edits.why_correct: Bacillus cereus spores survive cooking of rice and germinate if the rice is left at room temperature, producing a heat-stable emetic toxin. Brief reheating does not destroy the toxin, so vomiting starts within one to five hours of eating and usually resolves within a day. Cooked rice should be cooled quickly and refrigerated. Source: Food Standards Scotland, Rice: storing and reheating safely, accessed 2026.

edits.why_correct: Pearly penile papules are a common normal anatomical variant: small, uniform, dome-shaped papules arranged in rows around the corona. They are not infectious, not sexually transmitted and need no treatment. The main task is to recognise them and reassure the patient so that unnecessary treatment for warts is avoided. Source: Primary Care Dermatology Society, Pearly penile papules, 2021.

edits.stem:
A 44-year-old man sees his GP about a sore in the groove just behind the head of his penis, which he noticed about a week ago. It is a single ulcer with a clean base and a firm, rubbery edge, and it does not hurt. He has had several new male partners over the past three months.

Which is the most appropriate next step?

options.A: Prescribe topical clotrimazole and review in two weeks
options.B: Start oral aciclovir and review if not healing
options.C: Refer routinely to dermatology for a biopsy
options.D: Refer urgently to sexual health for syphilis testing
options.E: Apply a mild topical steroid and review in a month

edits.correct_answer: D. Refer urgently to sexual health for syphilis testing
edits.why_correct: A single painless indurated ulcer after recent new partners is a primary syphilitic chancre until proven otherwise. A sexual health service can test the lesion directly (dark-ground microscopy or PCR), send serology, screen for other infections including HIV, treat with benzathine penicillin and arrange partner notification. Prompt referral matters because the chancre heals on its own while the infection progresses. Source: NICE CKS, Syphilis, 2025.
